title: تاريخ جديد.. الجماهير تخلد قمة الهلال والقادسية برقم قياسي
summary: المباراة كانت مثالية داخل الملعب وخارجه
body: المباراة كانت مثالية داخل الملعب وخارجه خلدت الجماهير مباراة القمة التي جمعت بين فريقي الهلال والقادسية في دوري روشن السعودي برقم قياسي غير مسبوق. وفاز الهلال على القادسية بنتيجة 3-2 خلال المباراة التي جمعت بينهما، مساء أمس الجمعة ، على ملعب الأمير محمد بن فهد بالدمام، في الجولة الحادية عشرة من دوري روشن السعودي. وقالت صحيفة "الرياضية" السعودية إن المباراة شهدت رقمًا قياسيًا فيما يتعلق بالحضور الجماهيري في مدرجات ملعب الأمير محمد بن فهد بالدمام. وأوضحت الصحيفة أن المباراة شهدت حضور 20 ألفًا و207 مشجعين، وهو أقصى عدد مسموح بحضوره في مدرجات الملعب، حيث يمثل 91% من السعة الفعلية للمدرجات، مع إضافة النطاقات الأمنية العازلة للجماهير. ناقش الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة وبذلك أصبحت هذه المباراة هي صاحبة الحضور الجماهيري الأعلى في المنطقة الشرقية، متفوقةً على مباراة الاتحاد والاتفاق التي أقيمت في يونيو/حزيران 2022، بحضور 20 ألفًا و115 مشجعًا. يُذكر أن المباراة جمعت بين متصدري دوري روشن في الموسم الحالي، وانتهت بقفز الهلال إلى الصدارة برصيد 27 نقطة، بفارق نقطتين أمام القادسية الذي هبط إلى المركز الثالث، خلف النصر بفارق الأهداف. تذاكر مباريات دوري روشن السعودي اشتر تذكرتك الآن!

title: خابيير تيباس يعلّق على بيع 42% من أسهم نادي فالنسيا
summary: «إنه خبر إيجابي للغاية لنادي فالنسيا ولمدينة فالنسيا بأكملها»، هكذا صرّح رئيس لاليغا.

title: الاتحاد يستعيد نجمه في رحلة البحث عن أول فوز آسيوي
summary: هل ينجح "النمور"؟
body: هل ينجح "النمور"؟ استعاد نادي الاتحاد نجمه، في رحلته للبحث عن أول انتصار في الموسم الحالي من بطولة دوري أبطال آسيا للنخبة. ويحل الاتحاد ضيفًا على نفيتشي الأوزبكي، بعد غدٍ الإثنين، على ملعب الأخير، في الجولة الثالثة من مرحلة الدوري ببطولة دوري أبطال آسيا للنخبة. وقالت صحيفة "الرياضية" السعودية إن قائمة الفريق الجداوي للمباراة شهدت عودة الجناح الهولندي ستيفن بيرجوين، بعدما تعافى من الإصابة التي تعرض لها مؤخرًا. وتعرض بيرجوين لإصابة بالتهاب معوي، تسببت في غيابه عن مباراة الدرعية، أمس الجمعة، والتي انتهت بفوز "النمور" بثنائية نظيفة، في الجولة الحادية عشرة من دوري روشن السعودي. عودة الجناح السعودي مهمة للغاية بالنسبة للاتحاد، لا سيما وأنه لم يحقق أي انتصار في دوري أبطال آسيا للنخبة حتى الآن. تذاكر مباريات دوري روشن السعودي اشتر تذكرتك الآن! وتعادل "العميد" في مباراته الأولى مع الشمال القطري بهدف لمثله، فيما خسر المباراة الثانية على ملعب الإنماء بجدة بنتيجة 2-1 أمام شباب الأهلي الإماراتي. هذه النتائج السلبية جعلت وضع الاتحاد مخيبًا للآمال في البطولة الآسيوية، حيث يحتل المركز الحادي عشر برصيد نقطة، فيما يحتل الفريق الأوزبكي المركز السابع برصيد 3 نقاط. ناقش الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة

The dwarf reed snakes ( Pseudorabdion ) pull off this acrobatic feat by keeping their head in a relatively fixed position while rotating the rest of their body, according to a new study published Monday (Oct. 19) in the journal Current Biology . Researchers filmed the snakes from different angles to better understand the mechanics of the rolling, or cartwheeling, behavior. They found that the snakes were capable of reaching velocities of up to 12.1 feet per second (3.69 meters per second), which is much faster than they can slither (technically referred to as undulating locomotion). title: Will plants survive climate change? The 'Great Dying' reveals clues about their resilience.
summary: Plants can't easily pick up and move when environmental conditions get rough, so they've evolved strategies to weather harsh conditions in place. That could help some plants survive in the face of a warming climate.
body: About 251 million years ago, volcanic eruptions wiped out most life on Earth. For about a million years , the Siberian Traps in Russia spewed huge clouds of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, leading to the most severe extinction event in our planet's history. Equatorial temperatures spiked , making much of the land too hot for life. Meanwhile, the oceans became acidic and most of the creatures in them suffocated from lack of oxygen . Known as the Permian-Triassic mass extinction or the "Great Dying," it ultimately destroyed more than 90% of ocean life and 70% of terrestrial species . However, in a corner of what is now China, a refuge of pollen-producing plants avoided that fate and created an oasis for surviving animals. Research suggests that this was not the only place where plants were able to weather catastrophic climate change during the Great Dying, and that plants may have been better able to withstand the extinction event than other organisms. title: Climate change is literally altering the shape of our planet
summary: The melting of the poles is increasingly shifting Earth's shape at a faster rate, with the planet becoming more and more round.
body: Climate change is making Earth progressively rounder, new research finds. The findings are a signal of human-caused climate change, however, and tracking the shape of the Earth can help reveal just how much impact people are having on its ice caps. Our planet is not a perfect sphere. Because of its rotation, it is a bit flatter at the poles and bulges in the middle. But the new study reveals that Earth is getting rounder at an accelerated rate, largely due to shifts caused by the melting polar ice caps. This finding applies only to the solid parts of the planet; the ocean continues to bulge outward at the equator. The study, published Sept. 9 in the journal JGR Solid Earth , used direct measurements from the global navigation satellite system (GNSS) to track the planet's shape-shifting over time. This system provides direct measurements, but there are limits in how it can be used. For example, there are few GNSS stations near the North and South poles and few in remote oceans because they must be deployed on buoys. title: Surprising new pattern of groundwater loss may signal a turning point for the Colorado River Basin
summary: During an intense drought from 2020 to 2022, the Upper Colorado River Basin lost far more groundwater than the Lower Basin did, despite having much higher natural recharge.
body: Western states that were thought to be resistant to prolonged drought may be more vulnerable than scientists previously believed, a new analysis of groundwater reserves in the Colorado River Basin finds. Researchers revealed the four states that together make up the Upper Basin — Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming — lost almost twice as much groundwater as the Lower Basin did during an intense drought in the southwestern U.S. between 2020 and 2022. The finding was unexpected and might signal a turning point for the region, because the Upper Basin has long been seen as more resilient to dry spells than the Lower Basin, said Esther Oyedele , a doctoral student in geosciences at Virginia Tech and the study's first author. "The Upper Colorado River Basin has historically been considered more resilient because it receives more precipitation, particularly snowfall in the Rocky Mountains," Oyedele told Live Science in an email. "I think the important takeaway is that we should not assume that the Upper Basin will remain relatively resilient simply because it has historically received more precipitation and snowmelt." title: James Webb telescope discovers surprising trove of metals around the Milky Way's supermassive black hole
summary: New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope reveal a concentration of heavy metals near the Milky Way's central black hole. The discovery deepens a mystery about why our galaxy's black hole behaves the way it does.
body: The Milky Way's supermassive black hole is surrounded by a surprising trove of heavy metals, according to new observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The metals may offer new clues about how Earth got its share of heavy elements — but it could also make one of the greatest mysteries about our local black hole even harder to solve. In astronomy , metals refer to any element heavier than hydrogen or helium, with common examples including oxygen, carbon, iron or gold. These elements are forged through nuclear fusion in the hearts of stars that are reaching the ends of their lives, before being sprayed into space and incorporated into new generations of stars. Scientists say the material spotted by JWST likely came from supernovas ‪—‬ stellar explosions that blasted the metal into the region around Sagittarius A (Sgr A*), the monster black hole in the middle of our galaxy. The metals, detected as gas, appear to have the same composition as several nearby stars, which suggests both the stars and the gas originated at the same time. Fewer than 20 coins minted during Olaf's reign have ever been discovered, and the newfound coin is a "national treasure," according to a statement from the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History. body: Sailor Matt Rutherford has dreamed for several years of becoming the first person to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo, nonstop and unassisted. He finally set out from western Greenland on June 25 to achieve this goal, but threatening encounters with Russia's security agency less than two months later forced him to reverse course. Rutherford is the founder and executive director of the nonprofit environmental organization Ocean Research Project , which gathers and analyzes marine data from a sailboat. His route took him around the southern tip of Greenland, through the Denmark Strait and into the Greenland Sea. From there, he sailed through the Norwegian and Barents seas, and reached Russia's Novaya Zemlya archipelago in mid-August. He was planning to continue to Canada and end his journey where it started, but Russian officials halted him in his tracks and ordered him to turn around. On his way home, Rutherford told Live Science about his adventures and why he wants to complete this loop. title: Lightest known pair of neutron stars proves Einstein right yet again
summary: Einstein's theory of relativity just got put to the test by the lightest binary neutron star system ever discovered.
body: Astronomers have discovered the lightest known pair of neutron stars — two ultradense stellar remnants that circle each other every 2 hours, 22 minutes, veering toward an inevitable collision about 82 million years from now. By timing radio pulses from one of the stars, the researchers detected three subtle effects predicted by Albert Einstein 's general theory of relativity and found that the theory describes the pair's motion to within about 1% — proving the visionary physicist right yet again . The researchers published their findings Sept. 15 in the journal Physical Review Letters . Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars that exploded as supernovas. Each packs more mass than the sun into a ball roughly 12 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter. Some, called pulsars, spin rapidly and sweep beams of radio waves across the sky like cosmic lighthouses. Their rotation is so steady that their pulses work as extraordinarily precise clocks. Very few pulsars orbit another neutron star. body: Some people with depression sleep far more than average, wake up exhausted, habitually stay up late, and experience mood shifts with the seasons. A new study suggests that these symptoms may cluster in a distinct subtype of depression that's tied to the body's internal clock. While research has long linked a scrambled circadian rhythm to a risk of mood disorders, neuroscientists are now proposing that these disruptions define a specific form of depression that they call "circadian depression." First conceptualized in 2021 , the body-clock subtype may affect about 1 in 4 people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, the researchers estimate. In their new study, published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in The British Journal of Psychiatry , the team identified the subtype in about 2,600 people out of over 11,000 evaluated. "Circadian depression is a biologically informed subtype," said study co-author Emiliana Tonini , a neuroscientist at the University of Sydney. This includes California's San Andreas Fault, which is similarly tilted and likely capable of generating a 7.8 magnitude earthquake . Historically, scientists studying Alzheimer's disease have focused on two proteins that accumulate in patients' brains: amyloid-beta and tau. However, there's a "third thing that people didn't pay attention to, until recently," said study co-author Li-Huei Tsai , a neuroscientist at MIT. That third thing is the accumulation of droplets of fat, or lipids, in the brain, she told Live Science. The APOE gene makes proteins responsible for transporting fat around cells throughout the body and brain. A version of the gene called APOE4, which increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's three- to 12-fold, makes proteins that are less efficient at this function, Tsai said. title: Black Death had dramatic effect on species diversity as humans abandoned farmland, study finds
summary: Researchers have found that during the Black Death, when a third of Europe's population was wiped out, biodiversity fell. Understanding the farming practices of the time could help us increase diversity in modern agriculture.
body: When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes. The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317. This was followed by the Black Death , an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century . This finding has serious implications for the long-term survival of the iconic trees in a warming world, and their role in storing carbon from the atmosphere. California redwood ( Sequoia sempervirens ) forests are among the largest aboveground carbon stores on the planet. These towering trees are native to central and northern California , and evolved to take advantage of the region's historically mild weather . In recent decades, their range has contracted significantly . But climate change is threatening the health and function of these forests. The region has seen significant warming in recent decades, and faces more frequent extreme heat days , with temperatures spiking above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37 degrees Celsius). The cable, called Petal, will be funded and operated by Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta. When it comes online in 2029, the ocean-spanning cable will be the first to deliver petabit capacity — double the capacity of existing subsea cables of this length — across transoceanic distances, Meta representatives said in a statement . That's enough to allow 75% of the world's population to stream music at once. Petal will also be the first commercial subsea cable system to use multi-core fiber technology, according to the statement. Whereas conventional fiber strands typically contain a single core, each of Petal's fiber strands will contain two cores that carry optical signals in opposite directions, allowing a single strand to provide the capacity that would conventionally require a pair of single-core fibers. However, clues in residual sediments lodged inside Earth's crust hint at the lost grandeur of primordial snowcaps and summits. title: Physicists froze a 'necklace' of atoms — and witnessed a quantum phenomenon predicted 100 years ago
summary: Atoms confined to a single line can bind into clusters called Bethe strings. A new experiment points to a mix of many such clusters, though the evidence is still indirect.
body: "Necklaces" of ultracold atoms have provided new evidence to support a nearly 100-year-old quantum theory. In 1931, physicists were trying to use quantum mechanics to explain why some materials are magnetic. Then, a young physicist named Hans Bethe looked at a single row of electrons. Each electron's spin can point up or down. Bethe worked out the math for how such a row behaves and found that if a few spins in the row flip, they can stick together and travel down the row as a single unit. Decades later, physicists found that Bethe's method also works for larger particles moving along a line , such as atoms. If those particles attract each other, the math predicts they will bind into clusters called Bethe strings. Now, physicists have found evidence of these clusters in a line of ultracold atoms. The findings were published Aug. 29 in the journal Nature Communications . The discovery may not create new gadgets, but it addresses a fundamental mystery in physics.
